citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].

For a finite data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$, where $n\ge1$, let
$$\bar x_n:=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t.$$
Its **biased sample ACVF** is the zero-extended sequence on $\mathbb Z$ given by
$$\widehat\gamma_n(h):=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and $\widehat\gamma_n(h):=0$ for $|h|\ge n$. The absolute lag makes
$\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For comparison, define the **pair-count-normalized rescaling**
$$\widetilde\gamma_n(h):=\frac1{n-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and set it to zero for $|h|\ge n$. Its denominator is positive on the stated
domain. The names specify the denominator convention; they assert no
unbiasedness formula.

derivations.claim: Each $X_t$ is integrable because $2|X_t|\le1+X_t^2$ and the probability space has total mass one. Repeated application of [F3] gives $\mathbb E[\bar X_n]=\mu$. By [F2] and its cited covariance-bilinearity supplier, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=n^{-2}\sum_{s=1}^n\sum_{t=1}^n\operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t)$.

Fix a data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let $y_t=x_t-\bar x_n$ for $1\le t\le n$, and set $y_t=0$ otherwise. By [F4], for every $h\in\mathbb Z$, $\widehat\gamma_n(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathbb Z}y_ty_{t+h}$. The sum is finite because $y$ has finite support. Replacing $t$ by $t-h$ and commuting the real factors shows $\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For $s,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, [F1] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t)=\gamma(s-t)$. For each integer $h$ with $|h|<n$, exactly $n-|h|$ ordered pairs $(s,t)$ satisfy $s-t=h$, and no ordered pair has $|s-t|\ge n$. Grouping the finite sum in step 1.1 by $h=s-t$ proves the variance identity.

Under absolute covariance summability, every weight $n-|h|$ in the identity is between $0$ and $n$, so $0\le\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)\le n^{-2}\sum_{|h|<n}(n-|h|)|\gamma(h)|\le n^{-1}\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}|\gamma(h)|$.

Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E[\bar X_n]=\mu$. Therefore $\mathbb E[(\bar X_n-\mu)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)$, and the bound in step 3.1 tends to zero as $n\to\infty$. This is precisely $L^2$ consistency for the mean.

Let $(a_j)_{j\in J}$ be any finitely supported real coefficient family indexed by integers. Expanding the finite sums and using the evenness from step 1.2 gives $\sum_{j,k\in J}a_ja_k\widehat\gamma_n(j-k)=n^{-1}\sum_{u\in\mathbb Z}(\sum_{j\in J}a_jy_{u+j})^2\ge0$. Only finitely many terms on the right are nonzero, and every summand is a square. Thus every finite Toeplitz quadratic form of $\widehat\gamma_n$ is nonnegative.

citations.quote:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.
